2) Primary options we discussed: Hosted API (fast to integrate), Dedicated capacity (reserved GPU pools with isolation guarantees), Private VPC/on-prem (for strict regulatory requirements).

3) Main concern you raised: noisy-neighbor effects on shared pools — impact on tail latency and SLOs during peak traffic

Where we can help next: Marissa (solutions) will share a short note on how we mitigate noisy-neighbor risk across Hosted vs Dedicated, including isolation boundaries, SLO guarantees, and what telemetry you can expect. Hi Sophie — following up with the technical details we discussed. TL;DR: Hosted/shared has mitigations but not the same isolation guarantees as Dedicated; Dedicated gives stronger latency SLOs and isolation, and Private gives full network isolation and customer-managed keys.

Details: 
- Noisy-neighbor risk (what it is): On shared pools, other tenants can temporarily increase CPU/GPU scheduling contention or memory/IO pressure. That shows up most clearly in tail latency for small, latency-sensitive requests.

- Hosted (shared pool) mitigations:
  * Continuous traffic shaping and preemptive autoscaling to protect latency-sensitive workloads.
  * Prefix/KV caching to avoid repeated compute for common prompts.
  * Per-request routing policies (priority lanes for fast interactive requests).
  * Monitoring: per-tenant 95th/99th token latency dashboards; alerting if tail degrades.
  * Limitations: we do not provide physical hardware isolation — under extreme cross-tenant spikes there can be transient tail latency increases.

- Dedicated capacity:
  * Reserved GPU pool (customer-only instances) — strong isolation from noisy neighbors.
  * Configurable node pool sizing with capacity guarantees; we can commit on p95/p99 latency SLOs per workload profile in the contract.
  * Isolation boundaries: dedicated KV cache, no cross-tenant scheduling, isolated network egress paths.
  * SLA options: optional baked-in priority scheduling and fixed slot allocation for burst control.

- Private VPC / On-prem:
  * Full customer control: VPC peering, dedicated hardware if on-prem.
  * Redwood control plane can be restricted to customer network; KMS integration for keys.

- Observability & ops:
  * In all modes we expose per-route/model traces, per-token cost, and error dashboards.
  * For Dedicated we provide extended retention and a runbook for capacity errors.

Attachments: I attached a short PDF with typical latency SLOs we can commit to for Dedicated, plus a stub of SOC 2 artifacts you asked about.

If you want, we can sketch a mutual action plan and a committed capacity number that maps your 120M tokens/month to an appropriate Dedicated pool size and expected unit economics.

Best,

Hi Sophie — quick answers while we prep for the deep-dive: 

1) Dedicated SLOs and credits: yes — we can include a p95 latency SLO in the Dedicated contract for a given workload profile. The credit structure is standard: service credit proportional to minutes of violation beyond the threshold, with exceptions for force majeure. We'll provide precise numbers in the contract draft; Marissa included typical targets in the attached PDF.

2) Hosted historical incidence: for customers with interactive chat patterns, transient p99 spikes happen but are rare — on our shared pool customers with similar profiles we see p99 spikes > 2x baseline fewer than 3% of peak-hours per week. We can provide anonymized aggregated graphs during the deep-dive.

3) Migration path: moving from Hosted to Dedicated is seamless from an API/SDK perspective — no code changes required in most cases. The migration involves re-pointing your model endpoint to the Dedicated deployment (DNS/hostname swap) and a short warm-up period for KV cache; typical switch-over is sub-5 minutes if coordinated, or we can run a gradual cutover.

Next step: Priyom will send a calendar invite for Wed 8/5 09:00 PT and include a brief agenda: security checklist, performance benchmarks, and a proposed committed capacity number.

Regards,
Rishi Malhotra
VP Sales, Redwood Inference
